pages.x: At 7:58 in the morning of 26 December 2004 the seabed off the Indonesian island of Sumatra split along a crack more than 1,000 kilometres long, in an earthquake of magnitude 9.1, one of the strongest ever recorded. The sea floor heaved upwards, lifting the ocean above it. The whole planet shook.

Within about twenty minutes, waves up to 30 metres high struck Aceh, at the northern tip of Sumatra. In the city of Banda Aceh the water swept kilometres inland, carrying a power-station ship into the town. In Indonesia alone around 167,000 people died, and whole villages along the coast vanished.

The waves raced across the ocean at the speed of a jet. Two hours later they hit Sri Lanka and the east coast of India, where no one had warned anyone; in Sri Lanka one wave wrecked a crowded train, killing more than a thousand people. They hit Thai beaches full of holidaymakers, and seven hours later reached Somalia, 5,000 kilometres away.

On a beach in Thailand a ten-year-old British girl, Tilly Smith, saw the sea suddenly pull back and froth. She had learned about tsunamis in a geography lesson two weeks before, and told her parents. The beach was cleared, and about a hundred people were saved.

On Simeulue, an island close to the earthquake, people had passed down stories of the smong, a great wave that struck in 1907. When the sea drew back, they ran for the hills. Of some 78,000 islanders, only seven died.

It was the deadliest tsunami in recorded history, and a third of the dead were children. Thousands of tourists from Europe died too. More than a million and a half people lost their homes, and the world gave billions of dollars in aid.
In Aceh rebels had been fighting the Indonesian army for nearly thirty years. The disaster brought both sides to talks, and in August 2005 they signed a peace that has held ever since.
In 2004 the Indian Ocean had no tsunami warning system. Scientists in Hawaii saw the earthquake, but had no way to warn the people in the waves' path.
pages.fx: Today sea-floor sensors, buoys and sirens watch over the ocean, so that its coasts get a warning within minutes of a great earthquake.

pages.x: The tsunami was one of the deadliest natural disasters in history, and the first filmed by so many ordinary people. It taught the world the lesson Tilly Smith had learned at school: if the sea suddenly pulls back, run for high ground.
